# Choosing a fixed-date thermal index

```{r a3-load}
E1 <- rev_tab("E1_fixed_date_candidates.csv")
E2 <- rev_tab("E2_post_spawn_indices.csv")
E2v <- rev_tab("E2_post_spawn_index_values.csv")
```

We replaced temp_90 with reach-year thermal indices computed over the same calendar window for every redd in a reach-year, so the index cannot depend on spawn date. The analyses are in `R/08_fixed-date-index.R`.

## Pre-spawn indices

We compared `r nrow(E1)` candidates: mean temperature over 30, 60 or 90 days ending on ten dates from 1 July to 15 August, plus the mean for 1 July--31 August and the maximum 7-day mean (MWAT) for June--September. Each was fit with the same model, spawn date ~ index + stream + year, with random intercepts for reach and reach-year (the reach-year term is explained in Section A5).

The data could not distinguish among the candidates: all fell within `r sprintf("%.0f", max(E1$dAIC_linear))` AIC units of the best (`r sprintf("%.0f", max(E1$dAIC_linear_noRY))` without the reach-year term), and the estimated effect ranged from `r sprintf("%.1f", min(E1$slope_lmer))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(E1$slope_lmer))` days per °C (@tbl-a3-e1, @fig-a3-e1). These indices are strongly correlated and rank reaches and years in nearly the same order. We therefore chose the index on biological grounds: the mean of the 60 days ending 16 July (18 May--16 July), which ends before the first observed redd (25 July) and so contains no temperatures experienced after any fish spawned. Because most adults arrive after this window, we interpret the index as a signature of each reach's thermal regime, not as the temperature individual fish experienced.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a3-e1
#| tbl-cap: "Candidate fixed-date thermal indices ranked by AIC. Slope is the linear effect (SE) from spawn date ~ index + stream + year with reach and reach-year random intercepts. Pre-spawn: window ends before the first observed redd."
E1 |>
  arrange(dAIC_linear) |>
  transmute(Index = index |> str_replace("mean(\\d+)_end", "\\1-d mean ending ") |>
              str_replace("_", " ") ,
            `Pre-spawn` = ifelse(pre_spawn, "yes", "no"),
            `ΔAIC` = sprintf("%.1f", dAIC_linear),
            `ΔAIC (no reach-year term)` = sprintf("%.1f", dAIC_linear_noRY),
            `Slope (d per °C)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", slope_lmer, slope_lmer_se),
            `R² marginal` = sprintf("%.3f", R2m_linear),
            `r (reach-year means)` = sprintf("%.2f", r_reach_year)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = "llrrrrr") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "scale_down", font_size = 7.5)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-a3-e1
#| fig-cap: "Fit (ΔAIC), effect size (± 2 SE) and correlation with reach-year mean spawn date for fixed-date indices of 30, 60 and 90 days, by window end date. Dashed line: first observed redd."
#| out-width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics(rev_plot("E1_fixed_date_candidates.png"))
```

## Post-spawn (incubation) indices

Salmon may time spawning so that fry emerge in a favourable spring window, so that reaches with colder incubation spawn earlier (Heggberget 1988; Brannon et al. 2004). The original submission tested post-spawn windows that began on each redd's own spawn date, which carries the mirror image of the artefact in Section A2. We instead computed fixed-date reach-year means for fall (1 Sep--30 Nov), winter (1 Dec--28 Feb), spring (1 Mar--30 Apr) and the whole incubation period (1 Sep--30 Apr), and the number of days to emergence for a fixed reference spawn date (1 Sep or 15 Aug), using the Beacham and Murray (1990) Chinook emergence model (model 2) as implemented in hatchR (Sparks et al. 2019). For a 1 September spawn, predicted emergence ranged from `r format(as.Date("2002-09-01") + min(E2v$emerge_1Sep), "%d %b")` to `r format(as.Date("2002-09-01") + max(E2v$emerge_1Sep), "%d %b")` among reach-years.

On their own, all post-spawn indices predicted spawn timing in the direction the hypothesis predicts (warmer incubation, later spawning; @tbl-a3-e2). For example, spawn date shifted `r sprintf("%.2f", -E2$slope_alone[E2$index == "emerge_1Sep"])` days earlier for each additional day of predicted incubation, offsetting roughly a quarter of the among-reach difference in development time. However, post-spawn indices were strongly correlated with the pre-spawn index (r up to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(E2$r_with_prespawn_T)))`). When added to the final model they improved fit only because of Big Creek; without Big Creek, none improved fit and their effects were near zero (@tbl-a3-e2). The data are therefore consistent with incubation matching but cannot separate it from the summer thermal regime of a reach (see also Section A4).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a3-e2
#| tbl-cap: "Post-spawn (incubation) indices. Alone: spawn date ~ index + stream + year. Added: index added to the final model (Section A5), with all streams and without Big Creek. Slopes are days per °C, or days per day of predicted incubation for emergence indices. Negative ΔAIC = better fit."
E2 |>
  transmute(Index = label,
            `r with pre-spawn index` = sprintf("%.2f", r_with_prespawn_T),
            `Alone: slope (SE); ΔAIC vs pre-spawn` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f); %+.1f", slope_alone, se_alone, dAIC_alone_vs_prespawn_T),
            `Added to final: slope (SE); ΔAIC` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f); %+.1f", slope_added, se_added, dAIC_added_vs_final),
            `Added, no Big Creek: slope (SE); ΔAIC` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f); %+.1f", slope_added_noBig, se_added_noBig, dAIC_added_vs_final_noBig)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = "lrrrr") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 8) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "3.6cm") |> column_spec(3:5, width = "2.9cm")
```
